stops.name: Baalbek tower, disrobed and beaten bloody
stops.campa: Locked within the tower, Barbara is stripped and beaten by her father's hand until she lies in her own blood on the floor she once filled with broken idols. Dioscorus punishes the body of the daughter he cannot argue out of her God, striking her the way a man strikes a wall that will not fall, wound after wound, until he leaves her for dead or near it on the stone. Nothing in the room answers him: not the three windows, not the light through them, only his daughter's silence under the blows and her refusal, even bleeding, to unsay what she said.

stops.name: Baalbek tower, the wounds healed by morning
stops.campa: Barbara wakes in the locked room to find the wounds of the night before closed and whole, her skin unmarked where her father's blows opened it, as if the beating had been erased along with the night. It is the first of the healings that will punctuate every torture still to come: her faith answered each morning with a body restored, so that no single day's cruelty can be made to stand as the last word on her. Dioscorus, informed of it, does not relent; he escalates, and delivers her at last to the machinery of the state.

stops.name: Baalbek, delivered to the prefect Marcianus; torches and iron claws
stops.campa: After a grievous imprisonment Dioscorus hands his daughter over to Marcianus, the provincial prefect, to be broken by the machinery of Roman law where a father's fists have failed. She is stripped again, struck with whips and clubs until she stands in a pool of her own blood, her sides raked with claws of iron, and torches held to her flesh to burn away her faith along with her skin. The torches go out of themselves as they near her; her wounds, examined the next morning, are healed entire, and the soldiers who rub vinegar into her cuts cannot find where the cuts were.

stops.name: Baalbek, Juliana converted, tortured beside her
stops.campa: A young woman named Juliana, imprisoned already for her own confession of Christ, watches Barbara's wounds close overnight and is so struck by the sight that she declares herself ready to suffer whatever comes, come what may, for the same God who heals what the prefect's men break. Marcianus, seeing a second convert made out of his own torture chamber, orders Juliana bound and beaten alongside Barbara, and the two women go into the remaining torments together: one strengthened by the other's testimony, both refusing, under the same iron and the same fire, to unsay their faith.

stops.name: Baalbek, mutilation, burning, dragged through the streets
stops.campa: Marcianus orders what remains of mercy stripped away: Barbara is mutilated, her breasts cut off, her body burned with fire, and then dragged naked through the public streets of Heliopolis as a spectacle and a warning to any citizen who might follow her God. She is carried past the temple courts of her own childhood, past the tower with three windows still standing on its hill, and through it all her faith holds unwavering; each new cruelty leaves her recovered rather than broken, and the city that watches begins to understand that this prefect cannot win by inflicting pain.

stops.name: Baalbek, condemned to death by the sword
stops.campa: Marcianus, unable to break Barbara by torture and unwilling to be shamed further by her endurance, brings her before the judge's seat a final time and pronounces the sentence Roman law reserves for the unrepentant: death by the sword, beheading, outside the city walls. Dioscorus, present at the sentencing, hears the verdict pass on his own daughter and does not ask for clemency; he asks instead for the office of executioner, offering to do with his own hand what the state has ordered done, so that the last authority over her body remains, as it began, his.

stops.name: The mountain above Heliopolis, led out to the place of execution
stops.campa: Barbara and Juliana are led out of the city together to the mountainside, the same slope, tradition holds, where the rock once opened for her flight, to be beheaded outside the walls as the law requires. On the climb Barbara prays her last prayer aloud: that the Lord who formed heaven and earth hear all who keep memory of His name and of her passion, and not remember their sins, for He knows our fragility. It is the prayer that will make her, for a thousand years after, the saint invoked against a death that comes too suddenly for confession.
stops.quote: Lord Jesu Christ, which hast formed heaven and earth, I beseech thee to grant me thy grace and hear my prayer, that all they that have memory of thy name and my passion, I pray thee that thou wilt not remember their sins, for thou knowest our fragility.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara

stops.name: The mountainside, Dioscorus claims the sword
stops.campa: On the mountain Dioscorus takes up the sword himself rather than let a stranger's hand finish what his own hand began in the bath-house. He beheads his daughter on the fourth of December, the day the Church will keep as her feast for as long as it keeps feasts, while beside them the appointed executioner beheads Juliana. Barbara dies by the hand that built her tower, gave her two windows, and could not forgive her the third: the whole architecture of the father's love turned, at the very end, into the instrument of her death.

stops.name: The mountainside, the lightning, and Dioscorus burned to ash
stops.campa: As Dioscorus and Juliana's executioner come down from the mountain, the heavens open without warning and a fire falls from the sky: a bolt of lightning strikes Dioscorus where he walks and consumes him to ashes on the path, and a second bolt takes the man who beheaded Juliana. Marcianus, hearing how the two executioners died within the hour of the executions, is seized with such terror that he too dies of the fright. The court that condemned her does not survive the day of her death; the sky itself closes the account the law left open.

stops.name: Constantinople, the relics translated from Heliopolis
stops.campa: In the sixth century, as the empire that once tried her rebuilds itself as Christian Byzantium, the relics of the Great Martyr Barbara are translated from Heliopolis to Constantinople, carried out of the province where she was born and beheaded into the capital of the faith her father tried to wall out of his house. The tower with three windows has by now become an image known across the Greek-speaking world; the girl once dragged by the hair through Heliopolis's streets is received into the City of Constantine under incense and imperial ceremony, a martyr promoted at last to the center of the world that killed her.

stops.name: Kyiv, the relics at Saint Michael's Golden-Domed Monastery
stops.campa: Tradition brings the relics further still: a Byzantine princess named Barbara, said to be daughter of the Emperor Alexios Komnenos, marries a prince of Rus and carries the martyr's bones north with her into Kyiv, where they are enshrined at the Golden-Domed Monastery of Saint Michael. There they remain through the centuries of the Rus church, an Akathist sung before them every week, the hand of the saint kept in its own reliquary at the monastery's left side: the third sister of the essay's triad now resident in a city her own hagiography never imagined, still working the healing she worked in her father's tower.

stops.name: Regensburg, the Fourteen Holy Helpers gathered against the plague
stops.campa: In the dioceses of Regensburg, Bamberg, and Würzburg, amid the Black Death and the famine that rides beside it, the faithful begin to invoke a fixed company of fourteen saints together as a single wall against plague, sudden death, and the collapse of the ordinary protections of life. Barbara stands at the core of the group with Margaret and Catherine, the three virgin martyrs of the Levant, contemporaries born two hundred kilometers from one another, now recruited as captains in a company of celestial specialists, each with a proprietary power, invoked as a body against a century that has run out of other defenses.
